outline.description: Sets out the factual context from the officers’ body-camera footage, the sequence leading to the entry, and how those facts drove the procedural history up to the Seventh Circuit’s review.
subtopics: 911 report of domestic violence; stepdaughter reports threats to kill mother; early-morning response
Porch encounter: Lisa’s hesitation about children’s safety; initial refusal to let officers in; request framed as a need to check welfare; Lisa’s "Okay"
Facilitated entry: Lisa opens door, manages dogs, identifies locations of children and Coleman
Inside the home: locating Coleman, consensual pat-down, children’s statements about gun threats and arson threat
Search warrant obtained after entry; discovery of multiple firearms
Federal charge: 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(1) felon-in-possession
Motion to suppress: magistrate judge recommends denial; district court adopts, finding valid consent and no scope overreach
Conditional guilty plea preserving suppression challenge; appeal to Seventh Circuit
Role of bodycam video in fixing facts: Norville and Scott v. Harris principles

outline.chapter_title: Governing Fourth Amendment Law and Standards of Review
outline.description: Explains the consent doctrine, third-party authority, voluntariness and scope standards, and the appellate lens used by the Seventh Circuit.
subtopics: Consent as a well-established exception to the warrant requirement (Schneckloth; Bumper; Banks)
Third-party consent where consenting party shares common authority with defendant (Matlock; Cellitti)
Voluntariness assessed under totality of circumstances; typical factors (Figueroa-Espana; Han; Jones)
Scope of consent determined by objective reasonableness—what a reasonable person would understand from the exchange (Jimeno; Saucedo; Jackson)
Appellate review: clear-error review of findings on voluntariness and scope; deference to district court’s view of bodycam evidence (Jones; Norville; Scott v. Harris)

outline.chapter_title: Analysis I: Voluntariness of Lisa’s Consent to Enter
outline.description: Applies the totality-of-the-circumstances framework to the porch exchange and explains why the district court’s voluntariness finding survived clear-error review.
subtopics: Calm, concerned tone and demeanor of Officer Kizer; no show of force; short, conversational encounter
Lisa’s demonstrated ability to refuse—initial denial shows awareness and agency
No custody, no physical coercion, and only a brief interaction before consent
Implication that consent was optional: officer asked permission; Lisa earlier said no
The “need” phrasing—why urgency about child welfare did not convert the request into coercion (Hicks); court’s totality-based rejection of coercion claim
Lisa’s immediate, facilitative conduct after saying "Okay" (identifying bedrooms; addressing dogs) as confirming voluntary consent
Conclusion: no clear error in finding consent was freely and voluntarily given

outline.chapter_title: Analysis II: Scope of Consent and the Warranted Search
outline.description: Explains why the officers’ actions remained within the objectively reasonable scope of the consent to check child welfare and how that led to a separate warranted search.
subtopics: Objective reasonableness of scope: consent to check children’s safety implies locating all occupants and assessing risk
Permissible in-home actions: brief scan to find Coleman and the children; basic safety questions
Consensual pat-down of Coleman; distinction from any broader, non-consensual search
Children’s statements provided information supporting probable cause for a warrant
Independent warrant obtained after entry; firearms recovered under warrant, not by exceeding consent
Court’s conclusion: activities inside matched the consent’s purpose; no scope overreach
Doctrinal non-reliance: no need to reach exigent circumstances or inevitable discovery given valid consent and subsequent warrant

outline.chapter_title: Holding, Rules Distilled, and Practical Significance
outline.description: States the disposition and extracts the operative rules and lessons for practice and exams, especially in domestic-violence contexts with bodycam evidence.
subtopics: Disposition: Affirmance of denial of motion to suppress and resulting § 922(g)(1) conviction
Key rules: third-party consent valid if voluntary; scope defined by objective reasonableness of the exchange; clear-error deference on appeal
Bodycam impact: video can resolve factual disputes and underscore demeanor, timing, and absence of coercion
Language matters but context controls: statements like "we need to" are not per se coercive; courts look to tone, options given, and the person’s responses
Domestic-violence welfare checks: consent to check safety can reasonably include locating all persons and brief canvassing for threats
Practice pointers: ask clearly for permission; avoid commands; document consent and facilitative conduct; for defense, focus on totality, not isolated words
